blocks.text: 1. Model Versioning

blocks.alt: A trained model is assigned a version, making it fully traceable

blocks.text: The version-number concept has already appeared throughout both the Model Registry and Retraining Strategies topics, model v1, v2, v3, each one distinct and retrievable. Model Versioning takes that concept further, asking exactly what needs to be versioned together, as one single, coherent unit.

A model alone, just the serialized weights, is not the whole story that actually matters. Its code, its training data, and its configuration all need tracking together as well, since getting any one of these pieces out of sync quietly breaks both reproducibility and safe rollback, even if the model file itself remains perfectly intact.
2. The Four Parts of a Complete Version

blocks.alt: A model version tracks code, data, hyperparameters, and weights

blocks.text: A complete model version needs to capture the model artifact itself, the serialized file already covered in the Serialization topic, alongside the code version, the exact Git commit that actually trained it, pinning precisely which version of the training logic produced this specific result.

It also needs the data version, the exact dataset snapshot actually used, directly echoing the data versioning concern already raised in the Data Pipelines topic, and the configuration, the exact hyperparameters used, exactly the information already captured by Experiment Tracking. All four pieces together, not the model file alone, define what a single model version genuinely, completely means.

blocks.text: 3. A Semantic-Style Numbering Convention

blocks.alt: A version number runs major, minor, patch

blocks.text: A useful convention, borrowed directly from standard software versioning practice, uses a major, minor, and patch structure. A major version bump signals a fundamentally different architecture or feature set entirely, moving from v1 to v2 for instance, a change substantial enough that direct comparison to the previous major version may not even be meaningful.

A minor version bump signals a retraining on new data using the same underlying architecture, v1.1 to v1.2 for instance, while a patch version bump signals a small, targeted fix, a corrected preprocessing bug for instance, v1.1.0 to v1.1.1. This structure communicates, at a glance, roughly how significant a given version change actually is, without anyone needing to dig into the full version history to find out.

blocks.text: 4. The Immutability Principle

blocks.alt: A published version is never changed again

blocks.text: A core principle underlying reliable model versioning is that once a version is registered, it never changes afterward. There is no editing v3's stored artifact or its metadata after the fact, even to fix something that later turns out to be wrong.

A needed fix always becomes an entirely new version instead, v4 for instance, never a silent edit applied directly to v3's existing record. This immutability is precisely what makes any past version genuinely, reliably reproducible later, since a version that could theoretically change after the fact can never be fully trusted as an accurate historical record.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Silently patching a registered version in place, even for a seemingly minor correction, undermines the entire point of versioning. Anyone who already referenced that version number now has an inaccurate picture of what it actually contains.

blocks.text: 5. Model Lineage

blocks.alt: A parent model produces a retrained child model

blocks.text: This connects back to Experiment Tracking's link between a specific run and the model it produced. Model lineage tracks a further, related question: which version was this particular model actually retrained or fine-tuned from?

This traces a full chain across versions, v1 to v2 to v3 for instance, not merely each individual version considered in complete isolation from the others. Understanding this lineage is genuinely essential for understanding how a model's actual behavior has evolved over time, and for tracing a specific behavioral quirk back to the exact version where it first, actually appeared.
6. Comparing Versions Side by Side

Comparing two versions side by side reveals metric differences first: did accuracy genuinely improve, or actually regress, moving from v2 to v3? It also reveals data differences, whether the training data's distribution meaningfully shifted between the two versions being compared.

And it reveals configuration differences, exactly which specific hyperparameter changed between versions, and by how much, often the single most direct, actionable explanation for why two otherwise-similar versions actually behave differently in practice. This kind of side-by-side comparison turns an abstract version history into genuinely concrete, actionable insight.
7. The Real Storage Cost

blocks.alt: Many versions stored bring a real storage cost

blocks.text: This connects back to Joblib's compression option, already covered in the Model Deployment module. Storing every single version indefinitely carries a real, genuinely accumulating storage cost, especially for large models with correspondingly large serialized artifacts.

A practical retention policy keeps every Production version and recent versions readily available, while archiving or pruning very old, never-actually-deployed versions to more cost-efficient, colder storage, or removing them altogether once they are confidently no longer needed for any compliance or debugging purpose.
8. When Rigorous Versioning Genuinely Matters Most

Rigorous model versioning genuinely matters most in any regulated domain, finance or healthcare for instance, where auditors may genuinely require proof of exactly which model made a specific past decision, information that simply does not exist without disciplined versioning already in place beforehand.

It matters just as much for any team retraining models on a regular, ongoing cadence, since without genuine rigor here, past versions become effectively, permanently unrecoverable over time, exactly the same kind of loss already covered as a risk in the Experiment Tracking topic, but now applied specifically to the model artifacts themselves.
9. Worked Example
The example below implements a minimal model versioning record capturing all four tracked components together, with lineage linking one version to its parent.

code.content:
import hashlib
import json

class ModelVersion:
    def __init__(self, version, code_commit, data_snapshot, config, parent_version=None):
        self.version = version
        self.code_commit = code_commit
        self.data_snapshot = data_snapshot
        self.config = config
        self.parent_version = parent_version

    def fingerprint(self):
        payload = json.dumps({
            "code_commit": self.code_commit,
            "data_snapshot": self.data_snapshot,
            "config": self.config
        }, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

    def describe(self):
        lineage = f" (retrained from {self.parent_version})" if self.parent_version else " (initial version)"
        print(f"Version {self.version}{lineage}")
        print(f"  Code commit: {self.code_commit}")
        print(f"  Data snapshot: {self.data_snapshot}")
        print(f"  Config: {self.config}")
        print(f"  Fingerprint: {self.fingerprint()}")

v1 = ModelVersion("v1.0.0", code_commit="a3f9c1e", data_snapshot="2026-01-15-snapshot", config={"n_estimators": 100, "max_depth": 6})
v2 = ModelVersion("v1.1.0", code_commit="a3f9c1e", data_snapshot="2026-02-15-snapshot", config={"n_estimators": 100, "max_depth": 6}, parent_version="v1.0.0")

v1.describe()
print()
v2.describe()
print("\nNote: v2 shares v1's code and config but uses a newer data snapshot, a minor version bump")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The fingerprint in this example is a simple hash of the tracked metadata, a useful way to quickly detect whether two versions genuinely differ in their tracked components, or are functionally identical despite having different version numbers.

blocks.text: 10. Key Takeaways

items: Model Versioning tracks the model artifact, code version, data version, and configuration together as one unit.
A major.minor.patch convention communicates a version's significance at a glance.
Once registered, a version never changes; a needed fix always becomes a new version instead.
Model lineage traces a full chain across versions, essential for understanding how behavior evolved over time.
Comparing versions side by side reveals metric, data, and configuration differences, turning history into actionable insight.
Storing every version indefinitely has a real cost; a practical retention policy balances history against expense.
Rigorous versioning matters most in regulated domains and for any team retraining models on a regular cadence.
This connects the version concept already used throughout Model Registry and Retraining Strategies into one complete practice.
